title: NFC Pet Tags — NFC Forum Type 2 / ISO/IEC 14443-A / AAHA Universal Microchip Lookup / AVMA / EU 576/2013 Pet Passport Companion-Animal Identification
summary: NFC pet tags deliver external, tap-to-view identification that complements the ISO 11784/11785 implanted microchip baseline. The tag carries a resolvable URL (registry lookup or custom endpoint) or a direct vCard on NTAG21x silicon (NFC Forum Type 2, ISO/IEC 14443-A, 13.56 MHz). In the United States, AAHA Universal Pet Microchip Lookup (aaha.org/petmicrochiplookup) aggregates 24 participating registries — including HomeAgain (Merck), PetLink (Datamars), AKC Reunite, AVID PETtrac, 24PetWatch, Save This Life, Petkey, Found Animals Microchip Registry, InfoPET, BuddyID, BanfieldChip, and MyMicroChip. So an NFC tag URL that points to the owner's registry profile (or a vendor-hosted lost-pet portal) gives finders a zero-scanner path to reunion while the implant remains the regulated primary identifier. Outside the US, EU 576/2013 Pet Passport + Regulation 429/2016 Animal Health Law require an ISO 11784/11785 FDX-B transponder for cross-border travel, and an NFC collar tag supplies the day-to-day finder-facing layer. ProudTek supplies NTAG213 (144 bytes), NTAG215 (504 bytes), NTAG216 (888 bytes), and NTAG424 DNA (416 bytes with SUN CMAC AES-128 anti-cloning per NXP AN12196) in six form factors: 25 / 30 mm epoxy disc, laser-engraved 316L stainless pendant with embedded inlay, silicone slide-over sleeve, die-cut shape (bone / paw / heart) from 3,000-pcs MOQ, silicone wristband variant for multi-pet households, and a chin-strap sewn variant for working dogs. IP67 testing includes 1-hour soak in 2 ppm chlorinated water, 316L split-ring pull-test, -25 / +70 °C operating band, and 10-year UV-stabilised epoxy qualification. GDPR + CCPA + PIPL data-protection posture supplied (URL mode: registry-hosted; vCard mode: on-tag; password-lockable per NTAG21x 32-bit PWD or NTAG424 AES-128).

sections.title: Regulatory context: companion-animal ID is a two-layer problem
paragraphs: The American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) and the American Animal Hospital Association (AAHA) both position the ISO 11784/11785 FDX-B implanted microchip as the primary, permanent identifier for companion animals. The external collar tag is the finder-facing supplement: an AVMA 2010 lost-pet study (Weiss et al., JAVMA) documented that dogs with ID tags were recovered by owners 87-90 % of the time versus 22 % without external ID, while implanted microchips returned cats to owners 38 % of the time versus 1.8 % without. The two systems work together — the tag gets the pet home fastest when a neighbour finds it; the microchip gets it home when the collar has slipped.

NFC pet tags sit on the external layer. The chip is NTAG21x or NTAG424 DNA; the air interface is NFC Forum Type 2 over ISO/IEC 14443-A at 13.56 MHz; the reader is any NFC-enabled smartphone from iPhone 7 / Android 2015 onward with background read on iPhone XS and newer. For travel, the regulated primary identifier remains the FDX-B implant: EU 576/2013 Pet Passport and 429/2016 Animal Health Law require ISO 11784/11785 compliance for dogs, cats, and ferrets crossing EU borders; the UK Pet Travel Scheme retains the same rule post-Brexit; Australia DAFF, New Zealand MPI, Canada CFIA, and Japan MAFF all accept ISO FDX-B.

The AAHA Universal Pet Microchip Lookup (aaha.org/petmicrochiplookup), launched 2009 and maintained by AAHA as a non-commercial service, aggregates 24 US registries. When a vet or shelter scans a microchip, AAHA returns which registry holds the owner record. An NFC collar tag that encodes a URL pointing to the owner's registry profile, or to a vendor-hosted reunion portal linked to the AAHA lookup, gives a smartphone-equipped finder immediate access to the same reunion flow — without a $200 universal scanner or a trip to a vet.

sections.title: Operating reference — companion-animal estates
paragraphs: Pet retail chains sourcing NFC pet tags as checkout add-on commonly specify NTAG213 (URL-only) with retail blister packaging and 316L split rings; the reunion URL resolves to a vendor-hosted portal where the buyer enters owner + pet details at home. AVMA and AAHA position statements recommend pairing the tag with an ISO 11784/11785 FDX-B implant for permanent identification, so most retail kits bundle the tag with a voucher for a microchip appointment or a reminder to verify AAHA Universal Pet Microchip Lookup registration.

Veterinary chains deploying branded NFC tags as a vaccination-visit add-on typically specify NTAG216 with per-patient UID-keyed URLs (encoded template such as https://records.yourvet.com/pet/{UID}); the URL resolves to the clinic's patient portal with vaccine record, dietary notes, allergies, and emergency contact. The per-unit encoding is batched with 100 % read-verify and a COC that lists chip family, memory map, lock status, and encoded payload hash. Clinics pair the tag with the registered FDX-B implant and encourage owners to self-enrol in HomeAgain, PetLink, AKC Reunite, AVID, or 24PetWatch.

Animal shelters including NFC tags in adoption kits commonly use NTAG215 (URL + compact vCard hybrid). The URL points to the shelter's adoption-record portal; the vCard fallback carries the shelter's main phone number so a finder can call even offline. Shelters enrol the adoptee's ISO 11784/11785 implant in AKC Reunite (non-profit, universal enrolment) or Found Animals Microchip Registry (non-profit, free enrolment), both queryable through AAHA lookup.

Show-dog, service-animal, and working-dog programmes commonly specify the NTAG424 DNA variant with SUN CMAC AES-128 to prevent cloned-collar impersonation at competitions, in access-control flows at airports / courthouses / medical facilities (service animals under ADA), or on K-9 units where credentialling matters. The SUN endpoint validates per-tap signatures against the NXP key-diversification scheme in NXP AN12196, and a failed CMAC resolves to a 'tag integrity check failed' banner instead of the normal profile page.

International travellers and breeders exporting companion animals pair the NFC collar tag with the regulated ISO 11784/11785 FDX-B implant that EU 576/2013 Pet Passport, UK Pet Travel Scheme, Australia DAFF, New Zealand MPI, Canada CFIA, and Japan MAFF require for cross-border movement. The NFC tag is the finder-facing daily-use layer; the implant is the regulated identity.

sections.title: Why NTAG424 DNA SUN matters for service-animal and working-dog programmes

dataHighlight.heading: Per-tap SUN CMAC signature validates original tag against clones
dataHighlight.text: NTAG424 DNA implements the NXP Secure Unique NFC (SUN) feature described in NXP AN12196. Each tap computes an AES-128 CMAC over the UID + monotonic read counter + optional session data, appended to the URL as a dynamic query parameter. A cloned tag without access to the AES-128 diversified key produces an invalid CMAC and the landing endpoint rejects the read. For service-animal credentialling (ADA Title II / III), K-9 unit identification, and show-dog lineage verification, this is the difference between 'a tag that anyone can copy with a $30 phone writer' and 'a tag whose originality can be cryptographically asserted on every scan.'

sections.title: How NFC pet tags work
paragraphs: An NFC pet tag carries an NFC Forum Type 2 chip (NTAG213 / 215 / 216) or an NTAG424 DNA chip, operating on the ISO/IEC 14443-A air interface at 13.56 MHz. When a finder holds an NFC-enabled smartphone within 0-5 cm of the tag, the phone powers the chip inductively, reads the NDEF payload, and either opens the URL in the default browser or offers to save the vCard as a contact. Background reading (no app needed) works on iPhone XS and newer; older iPhones (7 / 8 / X) require the NFC reader tile in Control Center. Over 90 % of Android phones from 2015 onward include NFC, with background reading standard from Android 4.4 KitKat.

Unlike QR-code tags, NFC does not require a camera, does not require line-of-sight, does not require good lighting, and reads through a phone case. Unlike an ISO 11784/11785 implanted microchip, NFC does not require a $200 veterinary scanner — it reads with the phone the finder is already holding. The two layers are complementary: the microchip is the regulated permanent identifier (AVMA / AAHA primary ID; EU 576/2013 Pet Passport; UK Pet Travel Scheme; Australia DAFF; New Zealand MPI; Canada CFIA; Japan MAFF); the NFC collar tag is the finder-facing supplement that activates the fastest reunion path when a neighbour picks the pet up at the end of the street.

faq.question: Does an NFC pet tag replace the implanted microchip?
faq.answer: No. AVMA and AAHA both position the ISO 11784/11785 FDX-B implanted microchip as the permanent, primary identifier. The NFC collar tag is a finder-facing supplement that anyone with a smartphone can read — a neighbour who finds the pet at the end of the street reunites it in minutes without a veterinary scanner. The two layers are complementary: the tag handles 'found by neighbour,' the implant handles 'collar slipped and animal arrived at a shelter.' For EU / UK / Australia / New Zealand / Canada / Japan travel, the implant is the regulated identifier required by law; the tag rides alongside.

faq.question: What phones can read the tag?
faq.answer: All iPhones from iPhone 7 onward and >90 % of Android phones sold since 2015. Background reading (no app required — just unlock the phone and tap the tag) works on iPhone XS / XR and newer and on Android 4.4 KitKat and newer. On older iPhones (7 / 8 / X), the finder opens the NFC reader tile in Control Center. ISO/IEC 14443-A operating at 13.56 MHz with NFC Forum Type 2 encoding matches the universal smartphone NFC stack.

faq.question: What's the difference between NTAG213, 215, 216, and NTAG424 DNA?
faq.answer: NTAG213 has {chip:nxp-ntag-213:user_bytes} bytes of user memory — enough for a URL. NTAG215 has {chip:nxp-ntag-215:user_bytes} bytes — enough for a URL plus a compact vCard. NTAG216 has {chip:nxp-ntag-216:user_bytes} bytes — enough for a full vCard with owner contact, vet contact, medical notes, allergies, and emergency instructions. NTAG424 DNA has {chip:nxp-ntag-424-dna:user_bytes} bytes plus AES-128 SUN CMAC per-tap authentication (per NXP AN12196) — it validates that the physical tag is the original rather than a cloned copy, which matters for service animals, show dogs, K-9 units, and any programme where collar-tag impersonation would be problematic.

faq.question: Can the tag be updated?
faq.answer: URL-mode tags: the URL stays fixed but the page it points at is editable server-side anytime — update vet, address, phone, photo without touching the tag. vCard-mode tags: the NDEF record can be rewritten with any NFC writer app, up to 100,000 rewrite cycles. Both modes can be password-locked with the NTAG21x 32-bit PWD / 24-bit PACK mechanism to prevent unauthorised rewrites. NTAG424 DNA adds AES-128 authentication for cryptographic lock.

faq.question: Which registries work with the NFC tag URL?
faq.answer: The AAHA Universal Pet Microchip Lookup (aaha.org/petmicrochiplookup) aggregates 24 US registries including HomeAgain (Merck Animal Health), PetLink (Datamars), AKC Reunite, AVID PETtrac, 24PetWatch (PTZ Pet Insurance), Save This Life, Petkey, Found Animals Microchip Registry, InfoPET, BuddyID, MyMicroChip, and BanfieldChip. The NFC tag URL can resolve directly to the owner's registry profile page, or to a vendor-hosted reunion portal that cross-references the AAHA lookup. For international deployments, the tag URL complements the ISO 11784/11785 implant required by EU 576/2013, UK Pet Travel Scheme, Australia DAFF, New Zealand MPI, Canada CFIA, and Japan MAFF.
